question: When is it better to use embedding (nested documents) vs references (links) in MongoDB?

options.text: Embedding only for primitives, references for objects
options.explanation: Data type doesn't determine the choice. You can embed whole objects (delivery address in an order). The criteria are read patterns and data growth

options.text: Embedding -- for data read together and that doesn't grow unboundedly; References -- for growing collections and data needed separately
Always embed, because MongoDB is a document database and JOINs aren't needed
options.explanation: Embedding doesn't work for infinitely growing arrays -- MongoDB documents are limited to 16 MB. If a user has thousands of orders, embedding will overflow the document

options.text: Always use references, like in relational databases -- it's more reliable
options.explanation: References require additional queries ($lookup or populate). If data is always read together (e.g., address in an order), embedding is more efficient -- one query instead of two

question: Why does Redis Pub/Sub require a separate connection for the subscriber?

options.text: It's a recommendation, but you can use a single connection
options.explanation: This is not a recommendation but a protocol requirement. After SUBSCRIBE, the client enters subscriber mode and cannot perform GET/SET. Attempting this will cause an error

options.text: Redis doesn't support pub/sub and regular commands on the same port
options.explanation: Redis supports all commands on the same port. The limitation is at the connection level: after SUBSCRIBE, the connection is blocked for other commands

options.text: For increased throughput -- two connections are faster than one
options.explanation: The reason is not performance but the Redis protocol. In subscriber mode, the client can only subscribe/unsubscribe and receive messages. Any other command will return an error

options.text: After subscribing, the connection enters subscriber mode and can't execute other commands (GET, SET, etc.)

question: What does COLLSCAN in explain() MongoDB indicate and how to fix it?

options.text: COLLSCAN means an error -- the collection is corrupted
options.explanation: COLLSCAN is not an error, it's a scan method. It means MongoDB is checking every document. It works, but is slow on large collections

options.text: COLLSCAN means a full collection scan (O(n)) -- you need to create an index on the filter fields to get IXSCAN (O(log n))
You need to restart MongoDB to recalculate query plans
options.explanation: Restarting won't help -- MongoDB uses COLLSCAN because there's no suitable index. The solution is createIndex() on the fields used in find()

options.text: COLLSCAN is MongoDB's normal operating mode for small collections
options.explanation: Even for small collections, COLLSCAN is suboptimal. MongoDB automatically uses IXSCAN when a suitable index exists. For growing collections, COLLSCAN will become a bottleneck

question: What happens to a key in Redis if you don't set a TTL?

options.text: Nothing bad -- Redis manages memory automatically
options.explanation: Redis doesn't magically manage memory. Without TTL and without maxmemory-policy, keys accumulate infinitely. When using as cache, always set TTL via setEx

options.text: Redis automatically deletes the key after 24 hours
options.explanation: Redis does NOT delete keys automatically without TTL. A key without an expiration exists until explicitly DEL'd or Redis restarts (if there's no persistence)

options.text: The key lives forever until explicitly deleted -- this causes memory leaks when using Redis as cache
The key is deleted on memory overflow thanks to LRU
options.explanation: LRU eviction only works if maxmemory-policy is configured (default is noeviction). Without configuration, Redis just returns an OOM error. Better to always set TTL
